lessons.title: Polygons: interior and exterior angles
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name polygons by their number of sides
Find the sum of the interior angles of a polygon
Find interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
Decide which regular polygons fit round a point
reviewNotes: The hexagon drawing uses six vertices computed at 60° intervals.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Sum of angles
blocks.md: A polygon with n sides can be cut into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so the interior angles add up to:

blocks.title: Regular polygons
blocks.md: A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. Its exterior angles add up to 360°, so each exterior angle is $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ and each interior angle is $180^\circ - \frac{360^\circ}{n}$. At a vertex, interior + exterior = 180°.

blocks.title: Names
blocks.md: 3 sides: triangle; 4: quadrilateral; 5: pentagon; 6: hexagon; 7: heptagon; 8: octagon; 9: nonagon; 10: decagon; 12: dodecagon. In a **tessellation** shapes fit together with no gaps: the angles round each point must add up to 360°.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using n × 180 instead of (n − 2) × 180.
- Using the interior angle instead of the exterior angle to find the number of sides.
- Assuming every irregular polygon has equal angles.

blocks.title: Example 1: unknown angle
blocks.statement: Five angles of a hexagon are 110°, 120°, 130°, 140° and 150°. Find the sixth.
steps: The five known angles add up to 110 + 120 + 130 + 140 + 150 = 650°.

blocks.title: Example 2: regular polygon
blocks.statement: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 40°. How many sides has it and what is each interior angle? Can the polygon tessellate?
steps: 140 does not divide 360, so identical regular nonagons alone cannot fill the plane without gaps.

lessons.title: Bearings and scale drawing
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use scales on maps and scale drawings
reviewNotes: The bearing figure is schematic. In the ship example the bearing is computed with tan⁻¹ (right-angled trigonometry is formally taught in Form 3); check where the scheme introduces it.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Three-figure bearings
blocks.md: A **bearing** is an angle measured **clockwise from North**, always written with three figures: North = 000°, East = 090°, South = 180°, West = 270°. The bearing of B from A means: stand at A, face North, then turn clockwise to face B.

blocks.title: Back bearings
blocks.md: The bearing of A from B differs from the bearing of B from A by 180°. If B is on a bearing of 065° from A, then A is on a bearing of 065° + 180° = 245° from B. If the first bearing is more than 180°, **subtract** 180° instead.

blocks.caption: A at the centre, North dashed up, B on a bearing of 065° from A.
blocks.alt: A diagram with north line and a line from A to B at 65 degrees clockwise from north.

blocks.title: Scales
blocks.md: A map scale 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on the map stands for 50 000 cm = 500 m on the ground. To find a real distance multiply the map distance by the scale; for a scale drawing choose a convenient scale, such as 1 cm : 2 km, draw the north line at every point and measure bearings with a protractor.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Measuring anticlockwise instead of clockwise.
- Writing 65° instead of 065°.
- Measuring the angle from the wrong point: the bearing 'of B from A' starts at A.

blocks.title: Example 1: back bearing and scale
blocks.statement: B is on a bearing of 065° from A. Find the bearing of A from B. On a map with scale 1 : 50 000, A and B are 4 cm apart; find the real distance.

blocks.title: Example 2: ship
blocks.statement: A boat leaves port A and sails 12 km due east to B, then 5 km due north to C. Find AC and the bearing of C from A.
steps: Right-angled triangle: AC² = 12² + 5² = 169, so AC = 13 km.
Measured clockwise from North, the angle is tan⁻¹(east ÷ north) = tan⁻¹(12 ÷ 5) ≈ 67.4°.

lessons.title: Circles: circumference and area
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the parts of a circle
Use π = 22/7 or 3.14 as the question directs
Find perimeters and areas of shapes made from circles and rectangles
reviewNotes: Arc length and sector area are left for Form 3. Check which value of π the exam convention requires.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a circle
blocks.md: The **circumference** is the distance round the circle. The **radius** r goes from the centre to the circle, the **diameter** d = 2r goes through the centre. An **arc** is part of the circumference, a **chord** joins two points, and a **sector** is a slice like a pizza slice. The number π (about 3.14, or 22/7) is the ratio circumference ÷ diameter for every circle.

blocks.title: Formulae
blocks.md: Circumference and area of a circle of radius r:

blocks.caption: A circle with diameter d, radius r and the formulae for C and A.
blocks.alt: A circle with a dashed diameter and a red radius.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md: Check whether you are given the radius or the diameter (r = d ÷ 2). Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, otherwise use 3.14 or the π key; say which value you use. For a **semicircle**, take half of the circle but remember to add the diameter when you want the perimeter.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the diameter in A = πr² without halving it.
- Mixing up circumference (a length, in cm) and area (in cm²).
- Forgetting the straight edge when the perimeter of a semicircle is needed.

blocks.title: Example 1: a wheel
blocks.statement: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 70 cm (take π = 22/7). Find its circumference. How many turns does it make on a 1.1 km road?

blocks.title: Example 2: a compound shape
blocks.statement: A play area at Garoua is a rectangle 20 m by 14 m with a semicircle of diameter 14 m added on one short side (π = 22/7). Find its area and perimeter.
steps: Perimeter = 20 + 20 + 14 + 22 = 76 m (the diameter side is inside).

lessons.title: Volume and capacity of prisms and cylinders
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate the volume of cuboids, cubes and prisms
Calculate the volume of a cylinder
Convert between m³, cm³ and litres
Solve problems on tanks and containers
reviewNotes: Cones, pyramids and spheres are left for Form 3.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Volume formulae
blocks.md: The volume of a **prism** (any solid with a constant cross-section) is the area of the cross-section times the length. For a cuboid and a cylinder:
blocks.tex: V_{\text{cuboid}} = l \times w \times h \qquad V_{\text{cylinder}} = \pi r^2 h

blocks.title: Units of volume and capacity
blocks.md: 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. 1 litre = 1 000 cm³, so 1 m³ = 1 000 litres. Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³). **Capacity** is how much a container holds, in litres. Always convert all lengths to the same unit before multiplying.

blocks.caption: A cuboid tank 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m high.
blocks.alt: A drawing of a rectangular box with its three dimensions labelled.

blocks.title: Method for prisms
blocks.md: Step 1: find the area of the cross-section (for a triangle ½ × base × height). Step 2: multiply by the length of the prism. Step 3: write the unit. A triangular prism with base 6 cm, height 4 cm and length 10 cm has V = ½ × 6 × 4 × 10 = 120 cm³.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing volume in square units.
- Forgetting the ½ for a triangular cross-section.
- Mixing cm and m in the same product.

blocks.title: Example 1: a water tank
blocks.statement: A rectangular tank at Bamenda measures 2 m by 1.5 m by 1 m. Find its volume and how many litres it holds when full.

blocks.title: Example 2: cylinder
blocks.statement: A tin is a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm (π = 22/7). Find its volume in cm³ and litres.
